entries.title: Introduction to 1 Thessalonians

entries.keywords: who wrote 1 Thessalonians author date when written outline background

entries.title: Introduction to 2 Thessalonians
entries.blurb: A short follow-up letter to a persecuted church, correcting the claim that the Day of the Lord had already come and calling idle members back to work.
entries.keywords: who wrote 2 Thessalonians author date when written outline background

entries.title: Introduction to 1 Timothy
entries.blurb: A letter from Paul to his coworker Timothy in Ephesus on false teaching, worship, church leadership, and the life of God's household.
entries.keywords: who wrote 1 Timothy author date when written outline background

entries.title: Introduction to 2 Timothy
entries.blurb: Paul's last letter, written from a Roman prison as he faces death, urging Timothy to guard the gospel, endure suffering, and hand the faith on.
entries.keywords: who wrote 2 Timothy author date when written outline background

entries.title: Introduction to Titus
entries.blurb: A short letter from Paul to Titus on Crete about appointing faithful elders, silencing false teachers, and the good works that grace produces.
entries.keywords: who wrote Titus author date when written outline background

entries.title: Introduction to Philemon
entries.blurb: Paul's shortest letter: a personal appeal to a Christian slave owner to receive his returning slave, Onesimus, as a beloved brother.
entries.keywords: who wrote Philemon author date when written outline background

entries.title: Introduction to Hebrews
entries.blurb: An anonymous sermon in letter form, urging weary Christians to hold on because Jesus is the final word of God and the great high priest.
entries.keywords: who wrote Hebrews author date when written outline background

entries.title: Introduction to James
entries.blurb: A pastoral letter of hard-edged wisdom from James, the brother of Jesus, insisting that real faith shows itself in endurance, speech, mercy, and deeds.
entries.keywords: who wrote James author date when written outline background

entries.title: Introduction to 1 Peter
entries.blurb: A letter of hope from the apostle Peter to scattered believers in Asia Minor who were suffering as outsiders for the name of Christ.
entries.keywords: who wrote 1 Peter author date when written outline background

entries.title: Introduction to 2 Peter
entries.blurb: A farewell letter in Peter's name urging believers to grow in godliness, trust the apostolic witness, reject false teachers, and wait for the day of the Lord.
entries.keywords: who wrote 2 Peter author date when written outline background

entries.title: Introduction to 1 John
entries.blurb: A pastor's letter to shaken churches after a painful split, teaching them how to know God, how to know the truth about Jesus, and how to know they belong.
entries.keywords: who wrote 1 John author date when written outline background

entries.title: Introduction to 2 John
entries.blurb: A one-page letter from the elder to a chosen lady and her children, urging love that walks in God's commands and a door closed to teachers who deny Christ came in the flesh.
entries.keywords: who wrote 2 John author date when written outline background

entries.title: Introduction to 3 John
entries.blurb: A personal note from the elder to his friend Gaius, praising his hospitality to traveling missionaries and confronting Diotrephes, a church leader who loves to be first.
entries.keywords: who wrote 3 John author date when written outline background

entries.title: Introduction to Jude

entries.keywords: who wrote Jude author date when written outline background

entries.title: Introduction to Revelation

entries.keywords: who wrote Revelation author date when written outline background

entries.title: What the Bible Is
entries.blurb: A library of sixty-six books in two testaments and three languages: what is in it, how it is arranged, and how Jewish, Protestant, Catholic, and Orthodox Bibles differ.

entries.title: How the Books Were Chosen
entries.blurb: How the Old and New Testaments came to contain the books they do, why some Bibles include the Apocrypha, and what the early church looked for in a book.

entries.title: How We Got the Old Testament
entries.blurb: From scribes to the Masoretes, the Dead Sea Scrolls, the Septuagint, and the other ancient witnesses: how the Hebrew Bible reached us and how reliable it is.

entries.title: How We Got the New Testament
entries.blurb: Papyri, great codices, thousands of manuscripts, and the editions behind modern Bibles: what the differences are and what they do and do not change.

entries.title: Why Translations Differ
entries.blurb: Word-for-word and thought-for-thought, the history of the English Bible, and how to read small capitals, brackets, and footnotes.

entries.title: Chapters, Verses, and References
entries.blurb: Who added chapter and verse numbers, how to read a reference, and where Hebrew and English Bibles number verses differently.

entries.title: Reading the Stories
entries.blurb: How biblical narrative works: the narrator's restraint, repetition, type-scenes, and why the heroes are rarely models.

entries.title: Reading the Law
entries.blurb: Case law and command, the covenant setting, the ancient law codes around Israel, and how Christians have related the Law to Christ.

entries.title: Reading Hebrew Poetry
entries.blurb: Parallelism, imagery, acrostics, the kinds of psalms, and a glossary of the psalm headings.

entries.title: Reading the Wisdom Books
entries.blurb: Proverbs, Job, and Ecclesiastes: what a proverb is and is not, and how the three books argue with each other.

entries.title: Reading the Prophets
entries.blurb: Who the prophets were, the forms they used, prediction and fulfillment, and how to read an oracle in its own time.

entries.title: Reading Revelation and Daniel (Apocalyptic Writing)
entries.blurb: Daniel and Revelation in the family of ancient apocalypses: visions, symbols, numbers, and the main schools of interpretation.

entries.title: Reading the Gospels
entries.blurb: Ancient biography, four portraits of one Jesus, how the first three Gospels relate, and how John differs.

entries.title: Reading the Parables
entries.blurb: What a parable is, how Jesus used them, and the history of reading them from allegory to the present.

entries.title: Reading the Letters
entries.blurb: The ancient letter, rhetoric and diatribe, reading someone else's mail, and household codes.

entries.title: Reading Genealogies and Lists
entries.blurb: Why the Bible keeps records of names and numbers, what they did for their first readers, and what they teach now.

entries.title: Between the Testaments
entries.blurb: From Nehemiah to Jesus: Persians, Alexander, the Ptolemies and Seleucids, the Maccabees, the Hasmoneans, Rome, and Herod.

entries.title: Pharisees, Sadducees, and Others
entries.blurb: The Jewish groups and institutions of Jesus' day: Pharisees, Sadducees, Essenes, Zealots, Samaritans, scribes, the Sanhedrin, the temple, and the synagogue.

entries.title: The Kings of Israel and Judah
entries.blurb: Every king of the united and divided kingdoms with approximate dates, the prophets who spoke to them, and the empires around them.

entries.title: The Empires Around Israel
entries.blurb: Egypt, Assyria, Babylon, Persia, Greece, and Rome: when each ruled and where each touches the biblical story.

entries.title: The Herods and the Roman Governors
entries.blurb: The Herodian family and the Roman officials who governed Judea in the New Testament era.

entries.title: Weights, Measures, and Money
entries.blurb: Cubits, shekels, talents, denarii, and the rest, with modern equivalents and what they meant in daily life.

entries.title: The Calendar and Festivals
entries.blurb: The Hebrew months, the Sabbath and the pilgrim festivals, the Day of Atonement, and the later feasts of Purim and Hanukkah.

entries.title: Offerings, Priests, and Purity
entries.blurb: The five offerings of Leviticus, the priesthood, clean and unclean, and why the sacrificial system matters for reading the New Testament.

entries.title: Act One: Creation
entries.blurb: The Bible does not open with rules or with religion. It opens with a maker. In the beginning God speaks, and where there was nothing there is light, sky, sea, land, and every living thing.
entries.keywords: Genesis 1 to 2

entries.title: Act Two: The Fall
entries.blurb: There was one tree the people were told to leave alone, one place to trust God instead of grasping for themselves. A voice came into the garden and turned the gift into a suspicion.
entries.keywords: Genesis 3 to 11

entries.title: Act Three: Abraham and the Promise
entries.blurb: Into a world scattered and far from God, the maker speaks to one old man. Leave your country, God says to Abraham, and go to a land I will show you.
entries.keywords: Genesis 12 to 50

entries.title: Act Four: Exodus and Sinai
entries.blurb: Years go by and the family becomes a people, and the people become slaves. A new king of Egypt fears them and grinds them under hard labor and orders their sons drowned. They cry out, and God hears.
entries.keywords: Exodus to Deuteronomy

entries.title: Act Five: The Land and the Judges
entries.blurb: After Moses dies, Joshua leads the people across the Jordan into the land God had promised to Abraham long before. City by city they enter the inheritance.
entries.keywords: Joshua, Judges, Ruth

entries.title: Act Six: The Kingdom
entries.blurb: The people demand a king like the other nations have. Their first king, Saul, looks the part and then crumbles. So God chooses a shepherd boy, the youngest son of Jesse, a man after his own heart.
entries.keywords: Samuel, Kings, and Chronicles, from Saul to Jehoash

entries.title: Act Seven: The Prophets and Exile
entries.blurb: For generations God sends prophets to plead with his people. They are not fortune tellers.
entries.keywords: Kings, Chronicles, and the Prophets, to the Exile

entries.title: Act Eight: The Return and the Silence
entries.blurb: After seventy years, a door opens. The empire that conquered Babylon lets the exiles go home. A remnant returns to a ruined Jerusalem.
entries.keywords: Ezra, Nehemiah, Esther, Malachi, and the Years Between

entries.title: Act Nine: Christ, the Center
entries.blurb: The silence breaks with a baby. In a backwater town, in a feeding trough, the maker of the world is born as a child. Angels tell shepherds the news. Wise men follow a star.
entries.keywords: The Gospels

entries.title: Act Ten: The Church and the Spirit
entries.blurb: Before he returns to his Father, the risen Jesus gives his followers a charge. Go and make disciples of all nations. Then, just as the prophets had promised, God pours out his Spirit.
entries.keywords: Acts and the Letters

entries.title: Act Eleven: The New Creation
entries.blurb: The Bible ends where it began, in a garden, only now it is also a city, and it is better than the first. The book of Revelation pulls back the curtain on where the whole story is heading.
entries.keywords: Revelation

entries.title: God Speaks: Revelation and Scripture
entries.blurb: God makes himself known in creation, in his acts in history, in the words of the prophets and apostles, and supremely in his Son.

entries.title: Prophecy and Fulfillment
entries.blurb: The prophets spoke God's word into their own day, calling Israel back to the covenant, and they also spoke of what God would yet do.

entries.title: Scripture and Canon
entries.blurb: Which books belong in the Bible, and why? The Old Testament canon Jesus and the apostles received, the New Testament books the church recognized as apostolic over the first four centuries, and the…

entries.title: Who God Is
entries.blurb: Scripture never argues God into existence; it introduces him. He is the one living God, maker of everything, who is not part of the world he made and yet is present to every part of it.

entries.title: The Trinity
entries.blurb: The church confesses one God in three persons, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, equal in power and glory and never three gods.

entries.title: God's Character: Holiness, Love, Justice
entries.blurb: God's attributes are not parts of him but ways of naming who he is: holy, righteous, faithful, merciful, patient, wise, all-powerful, everywhere present, unchanging.

entries.title: The Names of God
entries.blurb: In the Bible a name says who someone is. God reveals himself by names and titles: God (Elohim), God Almighty (El Shaddai), the Most High, and above all the LORD (YHWH), the covenant name given to…

entries.title: The Glory of God
entries.blurb: God's glory is the weight and radiance of who he is, made visible.

entries.title: Creation
entries.blurb: God made everything that exists, freely and from nothing, and called it good. Creation is not divine and not an accident; it is a gift that depends on God at every moment.

entries.title: Providence
entries.blurb: God does not wind the world up and walk away. He sustains and governs all things, working through ordinary events and even through evil intentions to bring about his purposes.

entries.title: God's Sovereignty and Human Choice
entries.blurb: Scripture teaches both that God rules over all things and that human beings make real choices for which they are responsible.

entries.title: Election and Calling
entries.blurb: God chooses: Abraham, Israel, David, the apostles, and a people in Christ. Election in Scripture is always for a purpose, so that the chosen become a blessing to others.

entries.title: Angels, Satan, and Spiritual Powers
entries.blurb: Scripture speaks of created spiritual beings: angels who serve God and carry his messages, and powers who rebel against him, led by the one called Satan, the accuser.

entries.title: Humanity and the Image of God
entries.blurb: Human beings are made in the image of God, male and female, as embodied creatures given dignity, relationship, work, and rule over the earth under God.

entries.title: Sin and the Fall
entries.blurb: Sin is not only breaking rules; it is turning from God to ourselves, which bends every relationship we have. It enters the world in Genesis 3 and spreads through every human heart and society.

entries.title: Marriage, Family, and Sexuality
entries.blurb: Scripture begins with a marriage and ends with a wedding. It honors marriage between a man and a woman, singleness, and the household as places where faithfulness is learned.

entries.title: Work and Vocation
entries.blurb: Humanity was placed in the garden to work it and keep it before sin ever entered the world, so work belongs to creation, not to the curse.

entries.title: The Image of God
entries.blurb: Genesis 1:26-27 says God made humanity in his image and likeness.

entries.title: The Messiah
entries.blurb: The Old Testament plants promises of a coming deliverer: the offspring of the woman, the son of David, the servant who suffers, the son of man who receives the kingdom.

entries.title: The Incarnation
entries.blurb: The church confesses that the eternal Son of God became a man, Jesus of Nazareth, without ceasing to be God: one person with two natures, fully divine and fully human.

entries.title: Sacrifice and Atonement
entries.blurb: Atonement is how sinners are made one with God again. Israel's sacrifices taught that sin is deadly serious and that God himself provides a way to cover it.

entries.title: The Resurrection of Jesus
entries.blurb: The church confesses that Jesus was raised bodily from the dead on the third day, the event on which Paul says the whole faith stands or falls.

entries.title: Christ's Ascension and Reign
entries.blurb: After his resurrection Jesus ascended to the Father and now reigns at God's right hand, the place of all authority.

entries.title: Christ as Prophet, Priest, and King
entries.blurb: Israel had three anointed offices: the prophet who spoke God's word, the priest who offered sacrifice and interceded, and the king who ruled for God.

entries.title: Salvation by Grace Through Faith
entries.blurb: Salvation is God's rescue of sinners from sin, death, and judgment into life with him. It is a gift of grace received by faith, not wages earned.

entries.title: Justification
entries.blurb: To be justified is to be declared righteous by God, the judge. Paul teaches that sinners are justified as a gift, by God's grace, through faith in Christ, not by works of the law.

entries.title: New Birth
entries.blurb: Scripture describes salvation as a new beginning worked by God: a new heart and a new spirit in Ezekiel, being born from above by the Spirit in John, a new creation in Paul.

entries.title: Union with Christ
entries.blurb: Paul's favorite description of a Christian is someone in Christ. Believers are joined to Christ by the Spirit, so that his death, resurrection, righteousness, and inheritance become theirs.

entries.title: Sanctification and Growth
entries.blurb: To sanctify is to make holy. Scripture speaks of believers as already set apart for God and also as being changed, over a lifetime, into the likeness of Christ by the Spirit.

entries.title: Assurance and Perseverance
entries.blurb: The New Testament gives believers real assurance that God will finish what he began in them, and it also warns them to hold fast and not fall away.

entries.title: Faith and Faithfulness
entries.blurb: Faith is trust in God and his promises, not a leap in the dark. Abraham believed God and it was counted to him as righteousness.

entries.title: Repentance and Forgiveness
entries.blurb: Repentance is turning back to God, a change of mind and direction and not only regret. The prophets call Israel to return, and Jesus and the apostles call everyone to repent and believe.

entries.title: The Holy Spirit
entries.blurb: The Spirit is the Lord and giver of life, present at creation, empowering judges, kings, and prophets, and promised by the prophets for all God's people. At Pentecost he is poured out on the church.

entries.title: The Gifts of the Spirit
entries.blurb: The Spirit gives gifts to God's people for the good of others: teaching, serving, leading, giving, mercy, and others Paul lists in Romans 12, 1 Corinthians 12, and Ephesians 4.

entries.title: Covenant
entries.blurb: A covenant is a binding relationship sealed by promise and oath.

entries.title: The Law
entries.blurb: The law given at Sinai was God's instruction for a redeemed people, a way of life shaped by his holiness, not a ladder to earn rescue. Israel was rescued first and given the law second.

entries.title: Israel in God's Purpose
entries.blurb: God chose Israel to be his people and, through Abraham's family, to bless all nations. The New Testament wrestles with Israel's place after Christ, especially in Romans 9 to 11.

entries.title: Exile and Restoration
entries.blurb: Exile is one of the Bible's great patterns: Adam and Eve sent from the garden, Israel carried to Assyria and Babylon for breaking the covenant, and God's promise to gather and restore.

entries.title: Holiness
entries.blurb: God is holy, set apart in his purity and majesty, and he makes a people holy to belong to him.

entries.title: Tabernacle, Temple, and God's Presence
entries.blurb: God's desire to dwell with his people runs from Eden through the tabernacle and the Jerusalem temple to Jesus, who spoke of his body as a temple, and then to the church, which Paul calls God's temple…

entries.title: Sabbath and Rest
entries.blurb: God rested on the seventh day and gave Israel the Sabbath as a sign of the covenant and a gift of rest, for servants, strangers, and animals as well.

entries.title: The People of God and the Church
entries.blurb: God's purpose has always been a people: Israel, called to be a light to the nations, and then the church, Jew and Gentile together in Christ, called his body, his bride, and his temple.

entries.title: Baptism and the Lord's Supper
entries.blurb: Jesus gave his church two practices: baptism, the sign of entry into Christ, and the Lord's Supper, the meal that proclaims his death until he comes.

entries.title: Leadership and Office in the Church
entries.blurb: The New Testament describes elders or overseers who shepherd and teach, deacons who serve, and a pattern of leadership modeled on Jesus, who came not to be served but to serve.

entries.title: The Nations and Mission
entries.blurb: From the promise to Abraham that all families of the earth would be blessed, God's purpose reaches every nation.

entries.title: Worship
entries.blurb: Worship is the whole response of God's people to who he is and what he has done: sacrifice and festival in Israel, psalm and prayer, and in the New Testament the offering of one's whole life, gathered…

entries.title: Love of God and Neighbor
entries.blurb: Jesus named two commandments as the greatest: to love God with all one's heart, soul, mind, and strength, and to love one's neighbor as oneself.

entries.title: Prayer and Lament
entries.blurb: Prayer is speaking to the God who speaks. The Psalms give every kind of prayer words: praise, thanksgiving, confession, and lament that argues with God in faith.

entries.title: Wisdom
entries.blurb: Biblical wisdom is skill in living well in God's world, beginning with the fear of the LORD.

entries.title: The Fear of the LORD
entries.blurb: The fear of the LORD is reverent awe before God that shapes a whole life. Proverbs calls it the beginning of wisdom and knowledge.

entries.title: Suffering and Evil
entries.blurb: Scripture does not hide suffering. It gives whole books to it: Job, Lamentations, and many of the Psalms.

entries.title: Idolatry
entries.blurb: Idolatry is giving to anything created the trust, love, and worship that belong to God alone. In Scripture it ranges from carved images to greed, which Paul calls idolatry.

entries.title: Justice, the Poor, and the Stranger
entries.blurb: The God of the Bible defends the orphan, the widow, the poor, and the foreigner, and he requires his people to do the same.

entries.title: Money and Possessions
entries.blurb: Scripture treats wealth as a gift from God and a dangerous rival to him. It commands generosity, forbids exploitation, and warns that the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil.

entries.title: Government and the State
entries.blurb: Scripture speaks of rulers as servants of God for justice (Romans 13, 1 Peter 2) and also of rulers who become beasts that demand worship (Daniel 7, Revelation 13).

entries.title: The Kingdom of God
entries.blurb: The kingdom of God is his rule breaking into a rebel world to set it right. The Old Testament longs for it and the prophets foresee it. Jesus announces that it has come near in himself.

entries.title: Judgment and Justice
entries.blurb: Because God is good, he does not ignore evil. He judges nations and individuals in history and will judge the world in righteousness at the end.

entries.title: Resurrection and the Last Things
entries.blurb: Christian hope is not escape from the body but the resurrection of the body and a renewed creation. Christ's bodily resurrection is the first fruits of it.

entries.title: The Return of Christ
entries.blurb: The New Testament promises that Jesus will come again, visibly and in glory, to raise the dead, judge the world, and make all things new.

entries.title: The New Heavens and the New Earth
entries.blurb: The Bible's final hope is not escape from the world but its renewal: a new heaven and a new earth where God dwells with his people, death is gone, and every tear is wiped away.

entries.title: Death and the Intermediate State
entries.blurb: What happens between death and the resurrection? The Old Testament speaks of Sheol, the grave or realm of the dead; the New Testament speaks of being with Christ, which is far better, while still…

entries.title: Hell and Final Destinies
entries.blurb: Jesus spoke more often than anyone in Scripture about final judgment and Gehenna.

entries.keywords: Age of the Councils

entries.keywords: Age of the Councils

entries.title: Augustine of Hippo
entries.blurb: Bishop and theologian, 354 to 430. Augustine spent his youth chasing ambition, pleasure, and a string of philosophies, all while his mother prayed for him.
entries.keywords: Age of the Councils

entries.title: Benedict of Nursia
entries.blurb: Monk and founder, around 480 to 547. Benedict left the chaos of a collapsing Roman world to live as a hermit, then gathered followers and wrote a short, sane guidebook for life in community.

entries.title: First Council of Nicaea
entries.blurb: 325, Nicaea, in what is now Turkey. A priest named Arius taught that the Son of God was a created being, the highest creature but not God in the same sense the Father is.

entries.title: First Council of Constantinople
entries.blurb: 381, Constantinople, now Istanbul. The fight at Nicaea had settled the deity of the Son, but a new question pressed in.

entries.title: Council of Ephesus
entries.blurb: 431, Ephesus, in what is now Turkey. A bishop named Nestorius was teaching in a way that seemed to split Christ into two separate persons, one human and one divine, loosely joined.

entries.title: Council of Chalcedon
entries.blurb: 451, Chalcedon, near Constantinople. If Ephesus guarded against splitting Christ in two, a new error ran the other way.

entries.title: Second Council of Constantinople
entries.blurb: 553, Constantinople, now Istanbul. A hundred years after Chalcedon, disputes still simmered.

entries.title: Third Council of Constantinople
entries.blurb: 680, Constantinople, now Istanbul. A subtle question remained about Christ. If he is fully God and fully man, does he have one will or two?

entries.title: Second Council of Nicaea
entries.blurb: 787, Nicaea, in what is now Turkey. A bitter fight had broken out over images.

entries.title: The Great Schism
entries.blurb: 1054, Rome and Constantinople. This was not a council but a breaking apart.

entries.title: First Vatican Council
entries.blurb: 1869, Rome. Through the 1800s the Roman Catholic Church faced rising challenges from modern thought and political upheaval, and questions about the pope and his authority pressed for an answer.

entries.title: Second Vatican Council
entries.blurb: 1962, Rome. By the middle of the 1900s the Roman Catholic Church sought to speak afresh to a changed world without abandoning its faith.

entries.title: God, faith and reason
entries.blurb: The arguments for God's existence, set out step by step, with their strongest critics.
entries.keywords: case for the faith apologetics

entries.title: Why is there something rather than nothing? Couldn't the universe simply exist without God, or come from nothing by the laws of physics?
entries.blurb: The cosmological arguments start from a fact no one disputes, that there is a world at all, and ask what explains it.
entries.keywords: God, faith and reason Whatever we can conceive as existing we can conceive as not existing, so nothing exists necessarily, and the material universe may as well be the necessary being as God The universe is just there, and that's all; it needs no explanation outside itself The cosmological argument depends on the ontological argument for its whole strength Physical law can account for a universe coming to be from nothing, without a creator

entries.title: If everything needs a cause, who made God? And isn't it the believer's job to prove that God exists, not the unbeliever's job to disprove him?
entries.blurb: " is a fair question, and it would end the matter if the argument for God claimed that everything needs a cause. The serious arguments don't claim that.
entries.keywords: God, faith and reason If everything must have a cause, then God must have a cause; and if anything can be without a cause, it may as well be the world as God A God able to design a universe would be at least as complex and improbable as the universe, so he explains nothing The burden of proof lies on whoever affirms that God exists, and the reasonable starting point is not to believe

entries.title: Can anyone prove that God exists just by thinking about the idea of God? What is wrong with the ontological argument, and is anything right about it?
entries.blurb: Anselm of Canterbury argued, in a prayer written in 1077 and 1078, that God, rightly understood as that than which nothing greater can be conceived, can't exist in the mind alone.
entries.keywords: God, faith and reason Existence is not a real predicate, so no argument from the idea of God can show that God exists The same reasoning would prove that a perfect lost island exists

entries.title: Isn't morality just evolved instinct or social agreement? And doesn't Plato's Euthyphro show that goodness can't depend on God anyway?
entries.blurb: Nearly everyone, believer or not, lives as though some things are really wrong whatever anyone thinks.
entries.keywords: God, faith and reason The basic moral truths are necessary and need no foundation in God or anything else Objective moral values would be strange things unlike anything else in the world, so there are none; morality is invented If evolution shaped our moral judgments, it would be luck if they matched objective moral truths

entries.title: If our minds are products of unguided evolution, can we trust them? And isn't consciousness simply what brains do?
entries.blurb: Two facts about us are harder to explain than they look: that we are conscious, that there is something it is like to be us, and that we can reason our way to truths, including truths far from…
entries.keywords: God, faith and reason There is no inner theater where experience is shown to a self, and nothing in consciousness beyond the brain's own processing

entries.title: Can we trust the text of the New Testament?
entries.blurb: Manuscripts, variants and disputed passages, and what the evidence shows.
entries.keywords: case for the faith apologetics

entries.title: There are more differences among the manuscripts than words in the New Testament. So how can anyone trust it?
entries.blurb: The figure is true, and Christians shouldn't flinch from it.
entries.keywords: Can we trust the text of the New Testament? More variants than words; 200,000 to 400,000 (later estimates higher)

entries.title: We don't have the originals, only copies of copies. Isn't it a telephone game?
entries.blurb: We don't have the originals, and nobody should pretend otherwise.
entries.keywords: Can we trust the text of the New Testament? No originals; copies of copies; early scribes amateurs

entries.title: Two famous passages were not in the earliest Bibles: the ending of Mark and the woman caught in adultery. What else was added?
entries.blurb: It's true. The last twelve verses of Mark (16:9-20) and the story of the woman caught in adultery (John 7:53 to 8:11) are missing from the oldest complete manuscripts, and most scholars, believers…
entries.keywords: Can we trust the text of the New Testament? The long ending of Mark The woman caught in adultery The Johannine Comma Luke 22:43-44 added against docetism

entries.title: Did scribes change the text to make Jesus look more divine?
entries.blurb: Sometimes, yes. In a few places copyists changed a word or a phrase so that a passage said more plainly what they already believed about Christ, and in a few others they softened words that seemed to…
entries.keywords: Can we trust the text of the New Testament? Orthodox corruption (John 1:18, 1 Timothy 3:16, Luke 2:33, Luke 3:22) Hebrews 2:9, "apart from God"

entries.title: Christians say the New Testament is better preserved than Homer or Caesar. Is that true, and what does it prove?
entries.blurb: It's true, and it proves less than it's often made to. Counted honestly, the New Testament survives in more manuscripts, in more languages, and closer in time to its writing than any work of classical…
entries.keywords: Can we trust the text of the New Testament? Having more manuscripts than any other ancient book doesn't show what the originals said, still less that they are true

entries.title: Who decides what the Greek New Testament says, and was there ever a single original to find?
entries.blurb: No one decides it by say-so, and the work is done in the open.
entries.keywords: Can we trust the text of the New Testament? The search for one original text of the Gospels misunderstands how the early church handed them on "Original text" has several meanings, and the field has rarely said which it means

entries.title: Why do modern Bibles leave out verses the King James Version has? Have they taken words out of God's word?
entries.blurb: They haven't taken anything out of the text as it was first written, though it's easy to see why it looks that way.
entries.keywords: Can we trust the text of the New Testament? The Greek text behind the Revised Version and modern Bibles rests on a few corrupt manuscripts; the traditional text the church used is right The reading of the majority of manuscripts, the Byzantine text, is usually original

entries.title: The Bible has been translated so many times. Hasn't the meaning been lost along the way?
entries.blurb: No, because it hasn't been translated over and over in a chain.
entries.keywords: Can we trust the text of the New Testament? Most modern English Bibles explain the text instead of translating it

entries.title: Was Jesus angry or compassionate when he healed the leper in Mark 1:41? Did scribes soften him?
entries.blurb: Possibly, and this is one of the places where honest scholars still disagree. Nearly every manuscript of Mark says that when a leper begged to be made clean, Jesus was "moved with compassion".
entries.keywords: Can we trust the text of the New Testament? Mark 1:41 originally said Jesus became angry; scribes changed it to compassion

entries.title: Who wrote the Gospels and the New Testament, when, and who chose the books
entries.blurb: Who wrote the Gospels and the letters, when, and how the church came to its list of books.
entries.keywords: case for the faith apologetics

entries.title: The Gospels are anonymous. Weren't the names Matthew, Mark, Luke and John added later?
entries.blurb: Partly yes, and the part that's true matters less than it sounds.
entries.keywords: Who wrote the Gospels and the New Testament, when, and who chose the books The Gospels circulated without names; the names Matthew, Mark, Luke and John were attached in the second century to give them apostolic authority The disciples were unlettered Aramaic speakers who could not have written the Greek Gospels

entries.title: Weren't the Gospels written decades after Jesus by people who never met him?
entries.blurb: On the dating most scholars hold, they were written decades later, and at least two of their authors, on the church's own account, were not among Jesus' followers.
entries.keywords: Who wrote the Gospels and the New Testament, when, and who chose the books The Gospel writers were far removed from the events, never saw Jesus and had no contact with eyewitnesses Acts, and so Luke, was written in the early second century

entries.title: Before anything was written, the stories about Jesus were passed by word of mouth for decades. Isn't that a game of telephone?
entries.blurb: The stories did change in the telling, and the Gospels show it: the same event told with different details, the same saying in different words.
entries.keywords: Who wrote the Gospels and the New Testament, when, and who chose the books Memory is reconstructive, and the stories about Jesus were reshaped in each retelling before the Gospels were written Many Gospel stories and sayings were created by the early communities that used them Kenneth Bailey's model of informally controlled oral tradition is not supported by his own evidence

entries.title: There were other gospels: Thomas, Peter, Judas, Mary. Didn't the church pick four and suppress the rest?
entries.blurb: There were other gospels, and early Christianity was more varied than the church's later histories liked to admit.
entries.keywords: Who wrote the Gospels and the New Testament, when, and who chose the books The proto-orthodox party won the struggles of the second and third centuries, compiled the New Testament and wrote the history of its own victory In some regions of the early church what was later called heresy came first

entries.title: Weren't some New Testament letters forged in the names of Paul and Peter?
entries.blurb: Some New Testament letters may not have been written by the men whose names they carry, and the case for doubting them is serious, literary, and made by careful scholars of every conviction.
entries.keywords: Who wrote the Gospels and the New Testament, when, and who chose the books Several New Testament letters under the names of Paul and Peter were written by others who claimed to be them, and are forgeries Ancient pagan, Jewish and Christian writers treated a false claim of authorship as deceit, not as an accepted convention

entries.title: The Gospels were written by believers to make believers. What kind of writing are they, and does their kind make them history, legend or something in between?
entries.blurb: They are ancient biographies, the kind of book Greek and Roman readers called Lives, written by believers and shaped by Israel's Scriptures. That answer cuts both ways, and both edges should be felt.
entries.keywords: Who wrote the Gospels and the New Testament, when, and who chose the books The Gospels are not biographies but folk literature, units of community tradition strung together by editors

entries.title: If Matthew and Luke copied Mark, aren't the first three Gospels really one witness rather than three?
entries.blurb: Partly, and that part should be said first. Most scholars think Matthew and Luke used Mark, and the case for some copying among the first three Gospels is strong: long passages agree in order and in…
entries.keywords: Who wrote the Gospels and the New Testament, when, and who chose the books Matthew and Luke each used Mark and a lost collection of sayings, Q, so where they follow Mark they are not independent of him There was no Q: Luke used Matthew as well as Mark

entries.title: John's Gospel is so unlike the other three, with no parables, long speeches and a different calendar. Isn't it theology rather than history?
entries.blurb: " The differences from the first three Gospels are real and large.
entries.keywords: Who wrote the Gospels and the New Testament, when, and who chose the books Jesus' divine claims in John belong to John's distinctive theology, not to the historical record of what Jesus said John's Gospel is largely myth

entries.title: Didn't the emperor Constantine, or the Council of Nicaea in 325, decide which books went into the Bible?
entries.blurb: No. The Council of Nicaea in 325 dealt with Arius's teaching about the Son, with the date of Easter, with a schism in Egypt and with twenty rules of church order, and none of what survives from it…
entries.keywords: Who wrote the Gospels and the New Testament, when, and who chose the books The emperor Constantine had a new Bible made and left out the gospels that showed Jesus as a mortal man The party that won compiled the canonical books and told the story of its victory

entries.title: Paul never followed Jesus in his lifetime, rarely quotes him, and wrote before any Gospel. Didn't Paul, rather than Jesus, invent Christianity?
entries.blurb: The question has real force. Paul's letters are the earliest Christian writings we have, he quotes Jesus only a handful of times, he says his gospel came "by revelation" rather than from the apostles…
entries.keywords: Who wrote the Gospels and the New Testament, when, and who chose the books Paul's teaching that no one is justified by the law cannot be reconciled with Matthew's Jesus on the law and the judgment Paul was the second founder of Christianity

entries.title: Contradictions and hard passages
entries.blurb: The census, the two genealogies, the death of Judas, the day of the crucifixion and the numbers in Kings and Chronicles.
entries.keywords: case for the faith apologetics

entries.title: Luke says Jesus was born during a census taken while Quirinius governed Syria. Josephus dates that census to AD 6, about ten years after Herod died. Didn't Luke get it wrong?
entries.blurb: On the evidence historians can weigh, he may have, and an honest answer has to say so.
entries.keywords: Contradictions and hard passages Luke dated Jesus' birth by the census of Quirinius, which Josephus places in AD 6, a decade after Herod died, so Luke misdated it The census of Luke 2 is the famous census of AD 6, placed a decade too early

entries.title: Matthew and Luke give Jesus two different family trees, with different fathers for Joseph. Doesn't that show at least one of them was made up?
entries.blurb: The two lists really are different, and the church has known it since antiquity.
entries.keywords: Contradictions and hard passages Matthew and Luke give Joseph different fathers and Jesus different lines from David, so the genealogies contradict each other The two genealogies cannot be fully harmonized; each evangelist shaped the traditions he had for theological ends

entries.title: Matthew and Acts tell Judas's death differently: in one he takes his own life, in the other he falls headlong in a field he had bought. Can both be true?
entries.blurb: Perhaps, but not obviously, and the honest answer has to say both.
entries.keywords: Contradictions and hard passages Matthew and Acts give two incompatible accounts of how Judas died, so the two contradict each other

entries.title: Mark says Jesus ate the Passover with his disciples and was crucified at the third hour. John says he was sentenced on the day of Preparation for the Passover, about the sixth hour. Don't the Gospels disagree about when Jesus died?
entries.blurb: They seem to, on both the day and the hour, and the question isn't settled.
entries.keywords: Contradictions and hard passages The Synoptic Gospels put the crucifixion on the day after the Passover meal and John on the day the lambs were killed, so they contradict each other on the day Jesus died John moved the day and hour of the crucifixion so that Jesus would die as the Passover lambs were slaughtered

entries.title: Samuel and Kings tell the same history as Chronicles, but their numbers often disagree: 800,000 soldiers or 1,100,000, seven hundred charioteers or seven thousand, a king of twenty-two or forty-two. If the Bible can't keep its numbers straight, why trust it on anything?
entries.blurb: The differences are real, and some of them are larger than most readers know, because modern translations, the Berean Standard Bible among them, already smooth several of them by following a parallel…
entries.keywords: Contradictions and hard passages Comparing Kings and Chronicles with each other shows confusion and contradiction in the Bible

entries.title: The historical Jesus and the resurrection
entries.blurb: Whether Jesus lived, what he claimed, the empty tomb, the appearances and the virgin birth.
entries.keywords: case for the faith apologetics

entries.title: Did Jesus even exist? Isn't the evidence outside the Bible too thin to be sure?
entries.blurb: He almost certainly existed, and the case doesn't depend on believing the Gospels are inspired.
entries.keywords: The historical Jesus and the resurrection The first Christians believed in a heavenly Jesus known through visions and Scripture; the Gospels later placed him in history There was no historical man behind the Christ of the Gospels

entries.title: Was Jesus really buried in a known tomb, and was it found empty, or is that a later legend?
entries.blurb: This is the most disputed part of the historical case, and the doubts are serious.
entries.keywords: The historical Jesus and the resurrection Jesus was probably not given a decent burial in a known tomb, so the stories of an empty tomb arose later Jesus' body was probably dealt with as crucified bodies usually were, and the honorable burial by Joseph of Arimathea arose later

entries.title: Couldn't the disciples' Easter experiences be explained by grief, legend or fraud, or by Jesus surviving the cross?
entries.blurb: Each of those explanations has serious defenders, and each fits part of the evidence.
entries.keywords: The historical Jesus and the resurrection Jesus' body decayed, and the appearances were visions born of grief and guilt, beginning with Peter's Some of Jesus' followers sincerely had visions of him, of the kind bereaved people have, and persuaded the others

entries.title: The four Easter accounts disagree about who went to the tomb, how many angels were there and where Jesus appeared. Doesn't that show they can't be trusted?
entries.blurb: The differences are real, and some of them can't be smoothed away. The Gospels name different women, report one messenger or two, and set the appearances in Galilee, in Jerusalem or both.
entries.keywords: The historical Jesus and the resurrection The Gospels' accounts of the resurrection contradict one another, and harmonizing them only produces a story none of them tells The contradictions among the Easter stories show that they were invented

entries.title: Bart Ehrman says historians can't conclude that a miracle happened. Doesn't that mean the resurrection can never be a historical claim?
entries.blurb: Ehrman is right about something important. History deals in probabilities, its methods can't observe God acting, and no historical argument proves the resurrection.
entries.keywords: The historical Jesus and the resurrection Historians can establish only what probably happened, and a miracle is by definition the least probable event, so a historian as a historian can never conclude that one occurred Historical method judges by probability, analogy and correlation, and so cannot affirm an event without analogy

entries.title: Bart Ehrman argues that Jesus' first followers believed God had exalted a man to heaven, and only later that he had been God from the beginning. Didn't the church turn a Jewish preacher into God?
entries.blurb: Christian thinking about Jesus did grow. Nicaea's "of one substance with the Father" is not in the New Testament, and some early texts speak of Jesus being declared Son of God at his resurrection.
entries.keywords: The historical Jesus and the resurrection Jesus' first followers believed God had exalted a man at the resurrection; the belief that he was God from before creation came later Philippians 2 contrasts Christ with Adam and need not speak of a life before his birth

entries.title: In Matthew, Mark and Luke, Jesus never says "I am God." Isn't the claim that he did a product of John's Gospel, written decades later?
entries.blurb: It's true that in the first three Gospels Jesus never says in so many words that he is God, and historians differ over how much of John's long discourses reproduces his own words.
entries.keywords: The historical Jesus and the resurrection Jesus did not claim to be God; John's high view of him is a late development "Son of Man" in Jesus' Aramaic could be a modest way of saying "I", not a claim to Daniel's figure Jesus used "son of man" in its ordinary Aramaic sense, and the references to Daniel were added by the early church

entries.title: Isn't the virgin birth a legend, built on a mistranslation of Isaiah and borrowed from pagan stories of gods who fathered heroes?
entries.blurb: Parts of the objection are true and should be granted. Isaiah's Hebrew word, *almah*, means a young woman, not necessarily a virgin, and the sign was first given to King Ahaz.
entries.keywords: The historical Jesus and the resurrection Jesus was conceived in the ordinary way, possibly outside marriage, and the virgin birth arose later Matthew and Luke inherited a tradition of an illegitimate conception

entries.title: Jesus said "this generation will not pass away until all these things have happened." Didn't he wrongly predict that the world would end within his hearers' lifetime?
entries.blurb: The sayings are real, and they are hard. In Mark, Jesus says "this generation" will see "all these things," and in Mark and Matthew he says some standing with him will see the kingdom come before they…
entries.keywords: The historical Jesus and the resurrection Jesus expected the Son of Man to come before the Twelve returned from their mission, and the prediction was not fulfilled Jesus thought his second coming would occur before the death of all the people living at the time, and so was not superlatively wise

entries.title: Christians say the apostles died for their testimony, and that no one dies for a lie. How much do we actually know about how they died, and what would it prove?
entries.blurb: Less than many Christians claim, and less than popular books suggest.
entries.keywords: The historical Jesus and the resurrection The stories of the apostles' deaths are legends of a credulous antiquity; martyrdom was gradually bestowed on apostles beyond Peter, Paul and James The disciples sincerely had visions of Jesus after his death, so their sincerity shows nothing about whether he rose

entries.title: The Old Testament: history, archaeology, violence and law
entries.blurb: The exodus, the conquest, Daniel, the flood, the law and the charge of an angry God.
entries.keywords: case for the faith apologetics

entries.title: No Egyptian record mentions the exodus, and archaeologists have found no trace of two million people in the Sinai desert. Did it happen at all?
entries.blurb: The silence is real, and it shouldn't be explained away. No Egyptian text mentions Israel's slavery, the plagues or the departure, and no camp of a great multitude has been found in Sinai.
entries.keywords: The Old Testament: history, archaeology, violence and law Archaeology has found no trace of the exodus in Egypt or Sinai, and the story is best read as a later national epic Two million Israelites wandering forty years would have left remains in Sinai, and none have been found

entries.title: Archaeologists found no walled city at Jericho when Joshua would have come, and Ai was already a ruin. Wasn't the conquest of Canaan a legend?
entries.blurb: Archaeology has made a sudden conquest of the whole land in one generation hard to defend, and an honest answer should say so.
entries.keywords: The Old Testament: history, archaeology, violence and law Jericho's last walled city fell in the sixteenth century BC, and there was little or nothing there for Joshua to conquer Israel emerged gradually from within Canaan, and the conquest stories are later legend

entries.title: Deuteronomy tells Israel to leave nothing alive that breathes in the cities of Canaan. How can a good God command that, and how can anyone know he did?
entries.blurb: The command is in the text, and the moral objection to it is one Scripture itself teaches a reader to feel: "Fathers shall not be put to death for their children, nor children for their fathers"…
entries.keywords: The Old Testament: history, archaeology, violence and law A perfectly good God would not command the killing of children, so either God is not good or the Bible is wrong that he commanded it No one can be as certain that a voice is God's as that killing an innocent child is wrong

entries.title: Daniel's visions trace the Greek kings in detail down to Antiochus IV and then seem to go wrong about how he died. Wasn't the book written in the 160s BC, after the events it appears to predict?
entries.blurb: Most critical scholars think so, and the case is serious. Daniel 11 follows the wars of the Greek kings of Egypt and Syria closely down to the persecution of Antiochus IV in 167 BC, and then describes…
entries.keywords: The Old Testament: history, archaeology, violence and law Daniel was written by someone living under Antiochus Epiphanes, who related the past rather than foretelling the future Daniel was completed between 167 and 164 BC: its prophecy of the Greek kings is exact down to Antiochus IV and wrong about his death

entries.title: Babylon told of a great flood, a boat, the birds and a sacrifice long before Genesis was written. Didn't Genesis simply borrow a Babylonian myth?
entries.blurb: The likeness is real and close, and Christians shouldn't play it down.
entries.keywords: The Old Testament: history, archaeology, violence and law Much of the Old Testament, its flood story among it, came from Babylon The flood story came into the Bible from Babylon

entries.title: The last chapter of Deuteronomy tells of Moses' death and burial, God is called by different names in different stories, and some events are told twice. Weren't the first five books written by many hands, centuries after Moses?
entries.blurb: Some of them were, and the books themselves show it. Moses didn't write the account of his own death, and a few notes, like the Edomite kings who reigned "before any king reigned over the Israelites,"…
entries.keywords: The Old Testament: history, archaeology, violence and law The five books were woven from sources written centuries after Moses, and the priestly law came last, not first The five books were written by someone who lived long after Moses

entries.title: The God of the Old Testament sends floods and plagues and commands wars, and the God Jesus called Father is love. Isn't the God of the Old Testament angry and the God of the New loving, and aren't they really two different gods?
entries.blurb: The contrast is old, popular and false. It was taught in the second century by Marcion, who, as Irenaeus records, developed the teaching of an earlier man named Cerdo and set the God of the Jews…
entries.keywords: The Old Testament: history, archaeology, violence and law The God of the Old Testament is the most unpleasant character in all fiction, petty, unjust and unforgiving Keeping the Old Testament as canonical Scripture in nineteenth-century Protestantism was the result of religious and churchly inertia

entries.title: Leviticus forbids eating shellfish and wearing clothing made of two kinds of material, and Christians ignore those laws while quoting others from the same chapters. Why do Christians keep some Old Testament laws and not others?
entries.blurb: Because the New Testament itself drew a line, though not where careless quoting draws it.
entries.keywords: The Old Testament: history, archaeology, violence and law Christians claim God's covenant but keep neither sabbaths, festivals nor circumcision, and so do not obey his commandments Mark's Jesus kept the food laws, and 'all foods' means all foods the Torah permits

entries.title: God told Abraham to offer his son Isaac as a burnt offering, and Abraham set out to do it. Did God really command a father to kill his child, and how can a story like that be praised?
entries.blurb: This page weighs a hard story; it is never a model for harming anyone, and anyone who feels pressed to harm a child or themselves in God's name should turn to Find Help (/help) now.
entries.keywords: The Old Testament: history, archaeology, violence and law Abraham should have answered that he was certain he ought not to kill his son, but could never be certain that the voice was God's The binding of Isaac has taught three faiths to honor a father's willingness to sacrifice his child, and should no longer be held up as a model

entries.title: Archaeologists have found no trace of the exodus, a Jericho without walls, and little sign of a great kingdom under David and Solomon. Does archaeology confirm the Old Testament, or undermine it?
entries.blurb: Neither, in the way the question usually means. From the ninth century BC on, inscriptions written by Israel's neighbors and enemies name kings and events the Old Testament records: Omri of Israel on…
entries.keywords: The Old Testament: history, archaeology, violence and law Tenth-century Judah was a thinly settled highland chiefdom, and the Bible's picture of a kingdom under David and Solomon was magnified later

entries.title: Science
entries.blurb: Galileo, miracles, the beginning of the universe, evolution, the age of the earth, Adam, the mind and the brain, free will and near-death experiences.
entries.keywords: case for the faith apologetics

entries.title: Science keeps explaining what people once put down to God. Hasn't it made God unnecessary?
entries.blurb: Science has made one kind of god unnecessary, and Christians should be glad to see him go.
entries.keywords: Science Science and religion are incompatible in method: science can find out it is wrong, religion holds its claims by faith, scripture and authority Because a law like gravity exists, the universe can create itself from nothing, and no creator is needed Darwin made it possible for an atheist to explain biological design, removing the strongest reason for belief

entries.title: The church condemned Galileo. Hasn't religion always been at war with science?
entries.blurb: The church did condemn Galileo, and it was wrong to. In 1616 Rome's theologians judged the claim that the sun stands at the center "formally heretical," and in 1633 the Roman Inquisition found Galileo…
entries.keywords: Science Religion and science have been in conflict throughout history, with the church holding back the advance of knowledge The history of science is a history of warfare with dogmatic theology

entries.title: A miracle would break the laws of nature. Didn't David Hume show that no one can reasonably believe in one?
entries.blurb: Hume showed something important, and less than he is usually thought to have shown.
entries.keywords: Science No testimony is sufficient to establish a miracle unless its falsehood would be more miraculous than the fact it reports No human testimony can prove a miracle so as to make it a just foundation for a system of religion Hume's argument against miracles, rightly read, still stands against its modern critics

entries.title: Christians say the Big Bang and the fine-tuning of physics point to God. Can't physics explain both without him?
entries.blurb: Physics may yet explain some of it, and Christians should be careful not to claim more than the science gives.8 billion years ago, and physics doesn't yet know what, if anything, came before.
entries.keywords: Science Physics shows how a universe can arise from nothing, so the Big Bang needs no creator Fine-tuning may be explained by a multiverse of universes with different constants, of which we observe one that permits life A designer would be at least as improbable as the design it is offered to explain

entries.title: Hasn't evolution disproved Genesis, and with it the Christian story of creation and the fall?
entries.blurb: If its findings hold, evolution rules out some readings of Genesis, and it presses hard on questions Christians care about: death before human sin, and who Adam was.
entries.keywords: Science The evidence of fossils, biogeography and shared genes shows the common descent of living things, humans included Darwin removed the strongest reason to believe in a designer

entries.title: The sciences say the earth is about four and a half billion years old, and Bible chronologies put creation a few thousand years ago. How old is the earth, and does the Bible say?
entries.blurb: The sciences that measure it say about four and a half billion years, and they say why: radioactive elements decay at measured rates, and meteorites and rocks from the moon and the earth give ages…
entries.keywords: Science The Bible gave the church a full and definite chronology, and geology proved it wrong The plain sense of Genesis is six ordinary days a few thousand years ago, and any other reading bends Scripture to fit science

entries.title: Fossils and genetics trace human beings back through a long history in Africa, from a population that was never only two people. Doesn't that rule out Adam and Eve, and with them the fall and the need for a Savior?
entries.blurb: The evidence is real and should be stated at its strength. Fossils and genetics, as standard reference works set them out, place the origin of our species in Africa a few hundred thousand years ago…
entries.keywords: Science Human genetic diversity shows that our ancestral population never fell below several thousand, which rules out all humans descending from a single recent couple Paul's use of Adam reflects the assumptions of his time and need not bind modern readers

entries.title: Damage to the brain changes memory, character and even the sense of self, and neuroscience ties more of mental life to the brain every year. Hasn't science shown that the mind is just the brain, and that there is no soul?
entries.blurb: Neuroscience has shown that the mind depends on the brain, closely and in detail, and Christians should say so without hedging. It hasn't shown that the mind is nothing but the brain.
entries.keywords: Science The present gaps in explaining conscious experience reflect only the early stage of inquiry, not a barrier in reality

entries.title: Experiments show the brain preparing an action before a person is aware of deciding to act. Hasn't neuroscience shown that free will is an illusion, and with it moral responsibility?
entries.blurb: No. Benjamin Libet's experiments of the early 1980s found a build-up of brain activity, the readiness potential, before people reported the urge to make a simple movement, and some scientists…
entries.keywords: Science The experience of consciously willing an action is an illusion The conscious intention to move cannot be the true cause of an action, because it comes after the brain's readiness potential

entries.title: People revived after their hearts stopped report leaving their bodies, a light, and meeting relatives who had died. Do near-death experiences prove that there is life after death?
entries.blurb: They do not. If you are thinking about your own death or about ending your life, please don't carry it alone: the site's Find Help page (/help) lists places to turn now.
entries.keywords: Science Accurate perceptions reported during near-death experiences, which the senses could not have supplied, are evidence that a person can survive the body

entries.title: Evil, suffering and judgment
entries.blurb: The problem of evil in its logical and evidential forms, natural evil, God's hiddenness and hell.
entries.keywords: case for the faith apologetics

entries.title: If God is all-powerful and wholly good, why is there evil at all? Didn't J. L. Mackie show that the two can't both be true?
entries.blurb: This page weighs an argument; for someone who is hurting now, the pages on suffering (/wisdom/suffering) and on losing a child (/wisdom/losing-a-child), and Find Help (/help), are the better place to…
entries.keywords: Evil, suffering and judgment God's omnipotence, God's goodness and the existence of evil cannot all be true, so belief in God is positively irrational An all-powerful God could have made free people who always in fact choose the good, so the appeal to free will fails

entries.title: Even if God and evil don't contradict each other, doesn't so much suffering that serves no purpose anyone can see make God unlikely?
entries.blurb: This page weighs an argument; for someone who is hurting now, the pages on suffering (/wisdom/suffering) and on losing a child (/wisdom/losing-a-child), and Find Help (/help), are the better place to…
entries.keywords: Evil, suffering and judgment There is intense suffering, like a fawn's slow death in a forest fire, that an all-powerful, all-knowing being could have prevented without losing any greater good, so probably there is no such being

entries.title: Earthquakes, cancer and the suffering of animals over ages before there were any people aren't caused by anyone's choice. How can a good God allow them?
entries.blurb: This page weighs an argument; for someone facing illness or loss now, the pages on suffering (/wisdom/suffering) and on losing a child (/wisdom/losing-a-child), and Find Help (/help), are the better…
entries.keywords: Evil, suffering and judgment The pattern of pain and pleasure in nature is what we would expect if nothing behind nature cared about its creatures, and much less what we would expect if a good God made it No good and all-powerful God would have designed wasps whose young feed inside living caterpillars

entries.title: If a loving God existed, wouldn't he make himself known to everyone who is open to him? Don't sincere unbelievers show that there is no such God?
entries.blurb: This page weighs an argument; for someone who feels God's absence in grief or darkness now, the pages on suffering (/wisdom/suffering) and on losing a child (/wisdom/losing-a-child), and Find Help…
entries.keywords: Evil, suffering and judgment A perfectly loving God would make a relationship with himself possible for everyone capable of it who does not resist, so the existence of nonresistant unbelievers shows there is no such God

entries.title: How could a good God punish anyone forever? Isn't the doctrine of hell itself the worst problem of evil?
entries.blurb: This page weighs an argument; for someone afraid now, for themselves or for someone they love who has died, the pages on grief (/wisdom/grief) and on heaven and eternity (/wisdom/heaven-and-eternity)…
entries.keywords: Evil, suffering and judgment No one who is really profoundly humane can believe in everlasting punishment, so Christ's belief in hell is a defect in his moral character No sin committed by a finite creature in a life of ambiguity and ignorance could deserve an infinite penalty

entries.title: Morality, sexuality and the church's record
entries.blurb: The Crusades, the Inquisition, slavery, abuse and its cover-up, what the Bible says about homosexuality, women, abortion in the early church, Christian nationalism, and whether morality is only culture.
entries.keywords: case for the faith apologetics

entries.title: Weren't the Crusades a holy war of conquest, and don't they show what Christianity does when it has power?
entries.blurb: The Crusades were a holy war, preached by popes and fought under the cross, and the worst of what was done in them was done in Christ's name: the massacre of the Jewish communities of Worms and Mainz…
entries.keywords: Morality, sexuality and the church's record The Crusades were the most signal and durable monument of human folly, made possible by a church that offered holy war as an atonement for every violation of justice

entries.title: Christians tortured and burned people for what they believed. How can a faith that ran the Inquisition claim to be good?
entries.blurb: It can't claim innocence, and it shouldn't try. For centuries Catholic and Protestant authorities alike put people to death for heresy, and some of the church's greatest teachers wrote the arguments…
entries.keywords: Morality, sexuality and the church's record As soon as Christians were powerful enough to use the sword they did, with the stake and faggot too, and the persecutions came from belief in revelation itself

entries.title: Christian nations conquered the Americas and built the Atlantic slave trade, and their churches blessed both. Doesn't that discredit the faith they claimed?
entries.blurb: It discredits the churches that blessed them, and that has to be said before anything else. Popes granted Christian kings the right to enslave unbelievers and to divide newly found lands.
entries.keywords: Morality, sexuality and the church's record The Bible endorses slavery, and the slaveholders who quoted it were reading it, not misreading it

entries.title: Church leaders hid the sexual abuse of children and protected the abusers. How can anyone trust a church, or the faith it preaches, after that?
entries.blurb: If you have been harmed, or someone you love has, the site's Find Help page (/help) lists places to turn now, and if a child is in danger, call the police; the sexual abuse of a child is a crime to be…
entries.keywords: Morality, sexuality and the church's record Bishops turned their backs on victims and protected their priests

entries.title: Christopher Hitchens said that religion poisons everything. Hasn't religion caused more wars and cruelty than anything else in history?
entries.blurb: Religion has sanctified a great deal of cruelty, and Christianity has its full share: crusades, the stake, wars between Catholics and Protestants that laid waste whole regions of Europe.
entries.keywords: Morality, sexuality and the church's record Religion poisons everything, and its crimes, unlike those of atheist regimes, are committed in the name of God The persecutions and religious wars that laid Europe in blood and ashes came from belief in revelation itself

entries.title: What does the Bible say about homosexuality, and why do Christians disagree?
entries.blurb: If you are gay, or love someone who is, you are met with respect here. If these verses weigh on you, talk with a trusted pastor or friend. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
entries.keywords: Morality, sexuality and the church's record The Bible's passages on same-sex acts had exploitation and excess in view, and do not address faithful, committed same-sex relationships

entries.title: The Bible never mentions abortion. What did the first Christians believe about it, and about leaving unwanted infants to die?
entries.blurb: If you carry grief or guilt about a pregnancy, or about the loss of a child before or after birth, please know that you are met with gentleness here, not judgment. God knows your story too.
entries.keywords: Morality, sexuality and the church's record An abortion before sense and life have begun harms no one, and the Bible itself never forbids it

entries.title: The Bible tells wives to submit and women to keep silent, and the church kept women down for centuries. Is Christianity bad for women?
entries.blurb: Christians have often been bad for women, and they have used the Bible to do it. That has to be said first.
entries.keywords: Morality, sexuality and the church's record The Bible teaches that woman brought sin into the world and is to live in silence and subjection

entries.title: Every nation's laws rest on somebody's morals. Why shouldn't a Christian people want a Christian nation? Is Christian nationalism Christian?
entries.blurb: Loving your country is not the problem. Scripture assumes it, and tells believers to pray for their rulers and seek the good of the place where they live.
entries.keywords: Morality, sexuality and the church's record A Christian people should order its laws and customs as a Christian nation, for its earthly and heavenly good

entries.title: Morals differ from one culture to the next, and Nietzsche traced Christian values to the resentment of the weak. Isn't Christian morality just the product of its culture?
entries.blurb: Culture shapes how every people sees right and wrong, and Christians are no exception. That much should be granted at once.
entries.keywords: Morality, sexuality and the church's record Christian values are the resentment of the weak turned into a morality

entries.title: Other religions, and those who never heard
entries.blurb: Whether all religions say the same thing, Jesus as the only way, and those who never heard.
entries.keywords: case for the faith apologetics

entries.title: Aren't all religions basically the same, different paths up one mountain to the same God?
entries.blurb: The great religions share more than many Christians admit: prayer, mercy to the poor, a moral law that sounds alike in many tongues, and saints whose lives put the rest of us to shame.
entries.keywords: Other religions, and those who never heard The great religions are different culturally shaped responses to one ultimate Real, each a valid context of salvation and none the one and only

entries.title: Isn't it arrogant to say that Jesus is the only way to God, and that billions of sincere believers in other faiths are wrong?
entries.blurb: It can be said arrogantly, and Christians have often said it that way, with contempt and sometimes with an empire behind them. That is sin, and it should be named.
entries.keywords: Other religions, and those who never heard Those who hold that their own religion alone is true often show arbitrariness or arrogance Religious exclusivism is presumptuous and morally objectionable

entries.title: What about the people who never heard of Jesus? Would a just God condemn them for being born in the wrong place?
entries.blurb: If this question comes to you because of someone you loved who has died, the closing paragraph of this page is written for you, and nothing here speaks of any person's fate.
entries.keywords: Other religions, and those who never heard A just God would not deny salvation to devout people of other faiths, who are not to blame for their beliefs

entries.title: Jews and Muslims both confess one God and refuse to worship Jesus. Isn't Christianity the faith that strayed from the God of Abraham?
entries.blurb: Christianity, Judaism and Islam share more than most of their members know: one God, the Creator, who called Abraham, spoke through Moses and the prophets, gives his commands and will judge the world.
entries.keywords: Other religions, and those who never heard The unity of God is the keystone of Judaism, and God's word that there is no God beside him means that he has no son

entries.title: Aren't you only a Christian because of where you were born? If you'd grown up in another country, wouldn't you hold its religion instead?
entries.blurb: Very possibly, and the honest Christian should admit it. Where and to whom a person is born shapes what he first believes, about God and about almost everything else.
entries.keywords: Other religions, and those who never heard The same causes that make a man a Churchman in London would have made him a Buddhist or a Confucian in Peking The religion a person holds depends in the great majority of cases on where he was born

entries.title: Made on Purpose
entries.blurb: You were not an accident or a mistake. God made you on purpose, and He likes what He made.

entries.blurb: Being scared is not a sin or a failure. The verse doesn't say if I am afraid, it says when.
entries.keywords: Psalm 56:3-4

entries.keywords: Ephesians 4:32

entries.keywords: Colossians 3:13

entries.keywords: 1 Thessalonians 5:18

entries.title: Talking with God
entries.blurb: Prayer is talking with a Father who loves to hear you, with no magic words and no fancy speech required.
entries.keywords: Matthew 7:7

entries.title: A Light for the Path
entries.blurb: The Bible is how God talks to us. It's a light that shows us the way to go.
entries.keywords: Psalm 119:105

entries.title: Trusting Enough to Obey
entries.blurb: We obey God not to make him love us, but because we trust that he loves us and knows what is best.
entries.keywords: John 14:15

entries.title: Small Things with Great Love

entries.title: A Happiness That Holds

entries.title: Taking Care of What Is Not Yours

entries.keywords: 1 Corinthians 4:2

entries.title: Where It All Came From

entries.keywords: Deuteronomy 8:10-14 thanksgiving gratitude family devotion

entries.title: The One Who Came Back
entries.blurb: Leprosy meant living apart from everyone, even your own family. These men could only call to Jesus from a distance. Then, somewhere on the road, their skin was clean.
entries.keywords: Luke 17:14-18 thanksgiving gratitude family devotion

entries.title: Thanks in the Middle of It
entries.blurb: Paul wrote this to a young church that was suffering for following Jesus. He knew how hard things were for them. Look closely at one small word. He says to give thanks in every circumstance.
entries.keywords: 1 Thessalonians 5:16-18 thanksgiving gratitude family devotion

entries.title: The Year the Fig Tree Did Not Bud
entries.blurb: Habakkuk wrote this knowing an army was coming, and the verse before says his whole body shook with fear. No figs, no grapes, no olives, no grain. For a farmer, that is every paycheck gone at once.
entries.keywords: Habakkuk 3:17-18 thanksgiving gratitude family devotion

entries.title: The Guests Who Cannot Pay You Back
entries.blurb: Most of us make guest lists the way Jesus describes: friends, family, people who will ask us back.
entries.keywords: Luke 14:12-14 thanksgiving gratitude family devotion

entries.title: The Empty Chair
entries.blurb: Tomorrow some of us will set the table with a chair missing. Maybe someone died this year, or long ago and it still hurts. Maybe someone is far away, or our family has come apart.
entries.keywords: John 11:32-35 thanksgiving gratitude family devotion

entries.title: His Love Lasts Forever
entries.blurb: Psalm 136 has twenty-six verses, and every one ends the same way: his loving devotion endures forever. Try it at the table today.
entries.keywords: Psalm 136:1-3 thanksgiving gratitude family devotion

entries.title: The Long Wait Begins
entries.blurb: On the worst day in the story, when everything had already broken, God made a promise. Nothing about that afternoon got fixed, and the promise would take thousands of years to come true.
entries.keywords: Genesis 3:15 advent christmas family devotion

entries.title: A Family for the World
entries.blurb: Abram was old and had no children, and God told him his family would bless the whole world. That's a strange thing to promise an old man with an empty house.
entries.keywords: Genesis 12:1-3 advent christmas family devotion

entries.title: God Hears in the Dark
entries.blurb: The people had been slaves for four hundred years. Four hundred years is longer than the United States has existed. For all that time it must have looked like God wasn't listening.
entries.keywords: Exodus 3:7-8 advent christmas family devotion

entries.title: A King Who Lasts
entries.blurb: David was a real king with a real throne, and God told him a son from his line would reign forever. No human king lasts forever. They get old, they fail, they die.
entries.keywords: 2 Samuel 7:12-13 advent christmas family devotion

entries.title: Out of Bethlehem

entries.keywords: Micah 5:2 advent christmas family devotion

entries.title: A Child Is Given

entries.keywords: Isaiah 9:6 advent christmas family devotion

entries.title: A Light in Deep Darkness

entries.keywords: Isaiah 9:2 advent christmas family devotion

entries.title: A Branch from a Stump

entries.keywords: Isaiah 11:1 advent christmas family devotion

entries.title: Comfort My People

entries.keywords: Isaiah 40:1-3 advent christmas family devotion

entries.title: The Servant Who Carries It

entries.keywords: Isaiah 53:4-5 advent christmas family devotion

entries.title: A New Heart

entries.keywords: Ezekiel 36:26 advent christmas family devotion

entries.title: How Long, O Lord
